newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: ACPC's Barbosa says Brazil exceeded export curbs.
newsitem.headline: ACPC's Barbosa says Brazil exceeded export curbs.

text.p: The president of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) said Tuesday that Brazil had admitted to violating its ACPC export quotas over the last six months.

"I received official information from Brazil saying that in the last six months there was an excess of coffee exports," Rubens Barbosa told Reuters in an interview in this city in northwest Colombia where he joined in celebrations of the 70th anniversary of the National Coffee Growers' Federation.

Barbosa, himself a Brazilian, said that the excessive exports had only put his country about eight or nine percent above its assigned quotas, however, and added that he had already notified other ACPC countries of the violation.
"I transmitted this information to all member countries and I haven't received any commentary from any country," he said.

He did not elaborate but the potentially thorny issue is likely to come up again before September, when the ACPC is due to meet in London to thrash out new quotas agreed in June on a country-by-country basis.

Turning to other issues, Barbosa said the ACPC deserved at least "part of the credit" for the run-up in world coffee prices earlier this year because "the market has finally realized that there is strong political will behind its actions.
"The market today realizes that the ACPC is a player...because to a certain extent we can influence the market," he said. "In a sense we're now an institution that is well-recognized," he added.

He said that speculative investment funds and what he described as the erroneous "just-in-time" strategy of roasters had more to do with this year's hike in prices than anything the ACPC had done, however.

Barbosa, who has taken issue with what he sees as the U.S. Department of Agriculture's inflated estimates of Brazil's coffee crop, also said the Brazilian government hoped to introduce a new system to measure and provide official estimates of its coffee harvest by next year.
He did not elaborate but he insisted that "in the last few years our (Brazil's) estimates were much closer than the USDA's".
